Section 5.2 of Lock⁵ turns a bootstrap distribution into a one-line formula.
Whenever a bootstrap (or randomization) distribution for a statistic is
approximately **normal**, a confidence interval needs no percentiles at all:

$$\text{Sample statistic} \pm z^* \cdot SE$$

where $SE$ is the standard error of the statistic (read off the bootstrap
distribution, or given), and **$z^*$ is the endpoint of a standard normal
distribution** that leaves the confidence level $C$ between $-z^*$ and
$+z^*$ — **$z^* = 1.96$ for 95% confidence**, 1.645 for 90%, 2.326 for 98%,
2.576 for 99%; any other level comes from `norm.ppf(1 - (1 - C)/2)`. For a
single proportion the large-sample standard error is
$\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$ and for a single mean it is $s/\sqrt n$ (Chapter 6
develops these shortcut formulas in earnest); in this section the SE is simply
provided or estimated by bootstrapping. The normal-based interval and the
bootstrap **percentile interval** answer the same question two ways: they
agree closely when the bootstrap distribution is roughly symmetric and
normal-shaped, and drift apart when it is skewed — the percentile interval
follows the skew while the normal-based interval is always symmetric about the
statistic. The normal approximation is justified by **large samples**: for
proportions, counts of successes and failures comfortably above 10 and $n$
large; for means, $n \ge 30$ or data that are not strongly skewed.
The exercises below are from *Statistics: Unlocking the Power of Data*
(Lock⁵, 3rd ed., pp. 426–429). Skill Builders 5.34–5.35 find $z^*$ endpoints
for unusual confidence levels; 5.36–5.41 build
$\text{statistic} \pm z^* \cdot SE$ intervals from supplied standard errors;
the applied exercises 5.42–5.48 compute and interpret intervals for real
studies; 5.49–5.52 work the Online Dating Survey (Data 5.2); and the
technology exercises 5.53–5.57 compare percentile and normal-based intervals
on real Lock⁵ datasets. Every bootstrap below uses 10000 resamples (5000
where the book specifies) with seed 2026, so all intervals are reproducible.

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
from pathlib import Path
_root = Path.cwd()
while not (_root / "_quarto.yml").exists():
    _root = _root.parent
os.chdir(_root)
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

def zstar(conf):
    """Standard normal endpoint z* for a confidence level (0.95 -> 1.96)."""
    return float(stats.norm.ppf(1 - (1 - conf) / 2))

def ci_row(label, stat, se, conf, digits=3):
    """One-row summary of a normal-based interval: statistic ± z*·SE."""
    z = zstar(conf)
    m = z * se
    return pd.Series({label: round(float(stat), digits),
                      "Confidence level": f"{conf:.0%}",
                      "z*": round(z, 3),
                      "SE": se,
                      "Margin of error": round(m, digits),
                      "Interval": f"({stat - m:.{digits}f}, {stat + m:.{digits}f})"})
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Exercise 5.34

*(Skill Builder 1)* Find $z^*$ for (a) an 80% interval for a proportion,
(b) an 84% interval for a slope, (c) a 92% interval for a standard deviation.
$z^*$ depends only on the confidence level, not on the parameter: it is the
value with area $C$ between $-z^*$ and $z^*$ on a standard normal curve, i.e.
area $(1+C)/2$ to the left of $z^*$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.DataFrame({"Confidence level": ["80%", "84%", "92%"],
              "z* = norm.ppf(1 - (1 - C)/2)":
              [round(zstar(c / 100), 3) for c in (80, 84, 92)]}).to_string(index=False)
```

- **(a) $z^* = 1.28$** (80%: 0.90 to the left).
- **(b) $z^* = 1.41$** (84%: 0.92 to the left).
- **(c) $z^* = 1.75$** (92%: 0.96 to the left).

## Exercise 5.36

*(Skill Builder 2)* 95% interval for a proportion: $n = 100$,
$\hat p = 0.43$, $SE = 0.05$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
ci_row("Sample proportion", 0.43, 0.05, 0.95).to_string()
```

$\hat p \pm 1.96(0.05) = 0.43 \pm 0.098$. **We are 95% confident that the
population proportion $p$ is between 0.332 and 0.528.**

## Exercise 5.40

*(Skill Builder 2)* 95% interval for a difference in proportions
$p_1 - p_2$: $n_1 = 50$ with $\hat p_1 = 0.68$ and $n_2 = 80$ with
$\hat p_2 = 0.61$; $SE = 0.085$.

```{python}

```

$(\hat p_1 - \hat p_2) \pm 1.96(0.085) = 0.07 \pm 0.167$. **We are 95%

contains 0, so $p_1$ could equal $p_2$ (or even be smaller).

## Exercise 5.46

**Smoke-Free Legislation and Asthma.** Monthly records of the annualized
percent change in childhood asthma admissions in Scotland, before and after
the March 2006 smoke-free legislation: before, admissions were increasing at
a mean rate of 5.2% per year ($SE = 0.7$); after, decreasing at 18.2% per
year ($SE = 1.79$).

```{python}
#| echo: false
z95 = zstar(0.95)
pairs = [("Before legislation", 5.2, 0.7), ("After legislation", -18.2, 1.79)]
pd.DataFrame({"Period": [p[0] for p in pairs],
              "Statistic (% per year)": [p[1] for p in pairs],
              "SE": [p[2] for p in pairs],
              "Margin of error": [round(z95 * p[2], 3) for p in pairs],
              "95% CI": [f"({p[1] - z95 * p[2]:.2f}, {p[1] + z95 * p[2]:.2f})"
                         for p in pairs]}).to_string(index=False)
```

- **(a)** Before: $5.2 \pm 1.96(0.7) = 5.2 \pm 1.37$. **We are 95% confident
  that, before the legislation, childhood asthma admissions were increasing
  at a mean rate between 3.83 and 6.57 percent per year.**
- **(b)** After: $-18.2 \pm 1.96(1.79) = -18.2 \pm 3.51$. **We are 95%
  confident that, after the legislation, admissions were decreasing at a mean
  rate between 14.69 and 21.71 percent per year** (interval from −21.71 to
  −14.69).
- **(c) An observational study.** No random assignment — Scotland simply
  passed the legislation and admissions were recorded before and after.
- **(d) No.** Because the study is observational, confounding variables
  (other policy changes, weather, medical practice, secular trends) could
  contribute to the dramatic change; the evidence is compelling but cause and
  effect cannot be concluded from this design alone.

## Exercise 5.47

**How Much More Effective Is It to Test Yourself in Studying?** Students who
self-quiz recall a greater proportion of words than students who only read:
$\hat p_Q = 0.42$ vs $\hat p_R = 0.15$, with $SE \approx 0.07$ for the
difference. Find and interpret a 99% interval for $p_Q - p_R$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
ci_row("Difference in proportions", 0.42 - 0.15, 0.07, 0.99).to_string()
```

$(\hat p_Q - \hat p_R) \pm 2.576(0.07) = 0.27 \pm 0.18$. **We are 99%
confident that the proportion of correctly recalled words is between 0.090
and 0.450 higher for self-quiz students than for reading-only students** —
the self-testing advantage could be anywhere from about 9 to 45 percentage

## Exercise 5.49

**18- to 24-year-olds.** *(More on the Online Dating Survey, Data 5.2: a July
2015 random sample of US adults on whether they had ever used online
dating.)* Of 194 young adults aged 18 to 24, 53 had used online dating;
$SE = 0.032$. Find a 95% interval for the proportion of all US adults ages
18–24 who have used online dating.

```{python}
#| echo: false
n, succ = 194, 53
phat = succ / n
r = np.random.default_rng(2026)
simse = (r.binomial(n, phat, 5000) / n).std()
ci_row("Proportion, ages 18-24", phat, 0.032, 0.95).to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.Series({"phat = 53/194": round(phat, 4),
           "Formula SE sqrt(p(1-p)/n)": round(np.sqrt(phat * (1 - phat) / n), 4),
           "Simulated SE (5000 samples)": round(simse, 4),
           "SE given in the exercise": 0.032}).to_string()
```

$0.273 \pm 1.96(0.032) = 0.273 \pm 0.063$. **We are 95% confident that
between 0.210 and 0.336 — about 21% to 34% — of all US adults ages 18 to 24
have used online dating.** The three SE checks agree (0.032 each way), and
with roughly 53 successes and 141 failures the normal approximation is fine.

## Exercise 5.50

**55- to 64-year-olds.** Same survey: of 411 adults aged 55 to 64, 50 had
used online dating; $SE = 0.016$. Find a 95% interval for the proportion of
all US adults ages 55–64 who have used online dating.

```{python}
#| echo: false
n2, succ2 = 411, 50
phat2 = succ2 / n2
r = np.random.default_rng(2026)
simse2 = (r.binomial(n2, phat2, 5000) / n2).std()
ci_row("Proportion, ages 55-64", phat2, 0.016, 0.95).to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.Series({"phat = 50/411": round(phat2, 4),
           "Formula SE sqrt(p(1-p)/n)": round(np.sqrt(phat2 * (1 - phat2) / n2), 4),
           "Simulated SE (5000 samples)": round(simse2, 4),
           "SE given in the exercise": 0.016}).to_string()
```

$0.122 \pm 1.96(0.016) = 0.122 \pm 0.031$. **We are 95% confident that
between 0.090 and 0.153 — about 9% to 15% — of all US adults ages 55 to 64
have used online dating.** The two intervals (this and Exercise 5.49) do not
overlap: online dating is far more common among the young.

## Exercise 5.51

**College-Educated or Not?** Same survey: online-dating use by education
level (Table 5.2, entered directly).

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.DataFrame({"": ["Yes", "No", "Total"],
              "College": [157, 666, 823],
              "High school": [70, 565, 635],
              "Total": [227, 1231, 1458]}).to_string(index=False)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pc, phs = 157 / 823, 70 / 635
ci_row("College - high school or less", pc - phs, 0.019, 0.99).to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.Series({"College graduates": round(pc, 4),
           "High school or less": round(phs, 4),
           "Sample difference": round(pc - phs, 4),
           "Formula SE (for comparison)": round(
               np.sqrt(pc * (1 - pc) / 823 + phs * (1 - phs) / 635), 4)}).to_string()
```

- **(a)** College graduates: $157/823 = 0.191$. High school or less:
  $70/635 = 0.110$. Sample difference:
  $\hat p_C - \hat p_H = 0.081$.
- **(b)** $0.081 \pm 2.576(0.019) = 0.081 \pm 0.049$. **We are 99% confident
  that the difference in the proportions using online dating,
  $p_C - p_H$, is between 0.032 and 0.129.** (The formula SE,
  $\sqrt{\hat p_C(1-\hat p_C)/823 + \hat p_H(1-\hat p_H)/635} = 0.019$,
  matches the given SE.)
- **(c) No.** The 99% interval lies entirely above 0, so a difference of 0 is
  not in the range of plausible values: college graduates are more likely to
  have used online dating than those with a high school degree or less.

## Exercise 5.53

**Prices of Used Mustangs.** Data 3.4: $n = 25$ Mustangs offered for sale on
the Internet (`MustangPrice`, `Price` in $1000s). Construct a 95% interval
for the mean price two ways — (a) percentiles of a bootstrap distribution and
(b) a normal-based interval with the bootstrap SE — and compare.

*Data:* `data/ch03/MustangPrice.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/MustangPrice.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
mp = pd.read_csv("data/ch03/MustangPrice.csv")
price = mp.Price.to_numpy(float)
r = np.random.default_rng(2026)
bmean = np.array([r.choice(price, len(price), replace=True).mean()
                  for _ in range(10000)])
se = bmean.std()
lo_p, hi_p = np.percentile(bmean, [2.5, 97.5])
lo_n, hi_n = price.mean() - 1.96 * se, price.mean() + 1.96 * se
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Bootstrap distribution of the mean Mustang price with the percentile and normal-based 95 percent intervals marked
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
sns.histplot(x=bmean, bins=40, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
ax.axvline(price.mean(), color="black", lw=1.5)
for v in (lo_p, hi_p):
    ax.axvline(v, color="#c44e52", ls="--", lw=1.2)
for v in (lo_n, hi_n):
    ax.axvline(v, color="#55a868", ls=":", lw=1.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Bootstrap sample means ($1000s)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
pd.Series({"Observed mean": round(price.mean(), 3),
           "Bootstrap SE (10000 samples)": round(se, 3),
           "(a) 95% percentile interval": f"({lo_p:.2f}, {hi_p:.2f})",
           "(b) 95% normal interval": f"({lo_n:.2f}, {hi_n:.2f})"}).to_string()
```

- **(a)** The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the 10000 bootstrap means give
  **(11.93, 20.52)** — roughly \$11,900 to \$20,500.
- **(b)** $15.98 \pm 1.96(2.20)$ gives **(11.67, 20.29)** — roughly \$11,700
  to \$20,300.
- **Comparison:** the two intervals agree closely (the normal one is shifted
  slightly left, because the bootstrap distribution is mildly left-skewed),
  so the normal approximation works well here: both say the mean price of all
  such Internet Mustangs is plausibly anywhere from about \$11,700 to
  \$20,500.

## Exercise 5.54

**Predicting Price of Used Mustangs from Miles Driven.** Same 25 Mustangs:
predict `Price` (in $1000s) from `Miles` (in 1000s). (a) Find the regression
slope. (b) Bootstrap the slope and use the normal distribution to find a 98%
interval for the population slope.

```{python}
#| echo: false
xm, ym = mp.Miles.to_numpy(float), mp.Price.to_numpy(float)
dm = np.column_stack([xm, ym])
r = np.random.default_rng(2026)
bslope = np.empty(10000)
for i in range(10000):
    s = dm[r.choice(len(dm), len(dm), replace=True)]
    bslope[i] = np.polyfit(s[:, 0], s[:, 1], 1)[0]
slope = np.polyfit(xm, ym, 1)[0]
se_s = bslope.std()
lo_p98, hi_p98 = np.percentile(bslope, [1, 99])
z98 = zstar(0.98)
lo_n98, hi_n98 = slope - z98 * se_s, slope + z98 * se_s
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Bootstrap distribution of the regression slope for Price on Miles with the percentile and normal-based 98 percent intervals marked
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
sns.histplot(x=bslope, bins=40, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
ax.axvline(slope, color="black", lw=1.5)
for v in (lo_p98, hi_p98):
    ax.axvline(v, color="#c44e52", ls="--", lw=1.2)
for v in (lo_n98, hi_n98):
    ax.axvline(v, color="#55a868", ls=":", lw=1.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Bootstrap sample slopes ($1000s per 1000 miles)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
pd.Series({"(a) Slope": round(slope, 4),
           "Bootstrap SE (10000 samples)": round(se_s, 4),
           "(b) 98% normal interval": f"({lo_n98:.3f}, {hi_n98:.3f})",
           "98% percentile interval (comparison)": f"({lo_p98:.3f}, {hi_p98:.3f})"}).to_string()
```

- **(a) Slope = −0.219**: each additional 1000 miles on the odometer is
  associated with a predicted price about \$219 lower.
- **(b)** With the bootstrap SE ≈ 0.030 and $z^* = 2.33$ for 98% confidence:
  $-0.219 \pm 2.326(0.030)$ gives **(−0.289, −0.148)** — we are 98% confident
  that each extra 1000 miles lowers the mean price of all such Mustangs by
  between about \$148 and \$289. The percentile interval (−0.297, −0.150)
  agrees well, since the bootstrap slope distribution is nearly symmetric.

## Exercise 5.55

**Correlation between Time and Distance in Commuting.** For the $n = 500$
Atlanta commutes in `CommuteAtlanta`, the correlation between `Distance`
(miles) and `Time` (minutes) is $r = 0.807$. (a) Bootstrap to estimate the SE
of sample correlations. (b) Assuming the bootstrap correlations are normal,
find and interpret a 90% interval for the population correlation.

*Data:* `data/ch03/CommuteAtlanta.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/CommuteAtlanta.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
ca = pd.read_csv("data/ch03/CommuteAtlanta.csv")
dc = ca[["Distance", "Time"]].to_numpy(float)
r = np.random.default_rng(2026)
bcorr = np.array([np.corrcoef(dc[r.choice(len(dc), len(dc), replace=True)].T)[0, 1]
                  for _ in range(10000)])
rhat = ca.Distance.corr(ca.Time)
se_c = bcorr.std()
lo_p90, hi_p90 = np.percentile(bcorr, [5, 95])
z90 = zstar(0.90)
lo_n90, hi_n90 = rhat - z90 * se_c, rhat + z90 * se_c
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Bootstrap distribution of the correlation between Distance and Time with the percentile and normal-based 90 percent intervals marked
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
sns.histplot(x=bcorr, bins=40, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
ax.axvline(rhat, color="black", lw=1.5)
for v in (lo_p90, hi_p90):
    ax.axvline(v, color="#c44e52", ls="--", lw=1.2)
for v in (lo_n90, hi_n90):
    ax.axvline(v, color="#55a868", ls=":", lw=1.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Bootstrap sample correlations")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
pd.Series({"(a) Bootstrap SE (10000 samples)": round(se_c, 4),
           "(b) 90% normal interval": f"({lo_n90:.3f}, {hi_n90:.3f})",
           "90% percentile interval (comparison)": f"({lo_p90:.3f}, {hi_p90:.3f})"}).to_string()
```

- **(a)** Resampling the 500 (Distance, Time) pairs with replacement 10000
  times and recording each correlation gives **SE ≈ 0.036**.
- **(b)** $0.807 \pm 1.645(0.036) = 0.807 \pm 0.059$ gives **(0.747, 0.866)**.
  **We are 90% confident that the correlation between distance and time of
  Atlanta commutes is between 0.75 and 0.87** — a strong positive association:
  longer commutes take longer, though much of the scatter (traffic, route,
  mode) keeps it well below 1. The percentile interval (0.741, 0.860) is
  very close.

## Exercise 5.56

**Facebook.** A 2019 Pew random sample of US adults: the sample proportion
using Facebook was $\hat p = 0.69$ based on 1502 respondents.

- **(a)** Describe how to construct a bootstrap distribution to estimate the
  SE of the proportion: write each of the 1502 sample responses (about 69%
  "yes, use Facebook", 31% "no") on a slip, **draw 1502 slips with
  replacement** to form one bootstrap sample, record the proportion of yes
  answers, and repeat many times (say 5000); the standard deviation of those
  5000 bootstrap proportions estimates the SE. (This is equivalent to
  simulating 5000 samples of 1502 coin flips with success probability 0.69,
  whose SD matches $\sqrt{0.69(0.31)/1502}$.)
- **(b)** One such distribution (5000 samples) is normal with SE = 0.012.
  Find a 99% interval for the proportion of all US adults (in 2019) who use
  Facebook.

```{python}
#| echo: false
r = np.random.default_rng(2026)
simsfb = r.binomial(1502, 0.69, 5000) / 1502
ci_row("Proportion using Facebook", 0.69, 0.012, 0.99).to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.Series({"Formula SE sqrt(0.69 * 0.31 / 1502)":
           round(np.sqrt(0.69 * 0.31 / 1502), 4),
           "Simulated SE (5000 samples)": round(simsfb.std(), 4),
           "SE used in part (b)": 0.012}).to_string()
```

- **(b)** $0.69 \pm 2.576(0.012) = 0.69 \pm 0.031$ gives **(0.659, 0.721)**.
  **We are 99% confident that between 65.9% and 72.1% of US adults used
  Facebook in 2019.** (Our 5000-sample simulation gives SE = 0.012, matching
  the book's distribution; the formula SE is 0.0119.)

## Exercise 5.57

**Malevolent Uniforms in Football.** Figure 5.23 (reproduced below from our
own bootstrap) shows a bootstrap distribution of correlations between penalty
yards and uniform malevolence for the 28 NFL teams in `MalevolentUniformsNFL`:
mean 0.397, SE 0.205, 99% percentile interval −0.224 to 0.788. The original
sample correlation is $r = 0.43$.

*Data:* `data/ch05/MalevolentUniformsNFL.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/MalevolentUniformsNFL.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
mu = pd.read_csv("data/ch05/MalevolentUniformsNFL.csv")
du = mu[["NFL_Malevolence", "ZPenYds"]].to_numpy(float)
r = np.random.default_rng(2026)
bmu = np.empty(5000)
for i in range(5000):
    s = du[r.choice(28, 28, replace=True)]
    bmu[i] = np.corrcoef(s.T)[0, 1]
rhat_u = np.corrcoef(du.T)[0, 1]
se_u = bmu.std()
lo_p99, hi_p99 = np.percentile(bmu, [0.5, 99.5])
z99 = zstar(0.99)
lo_n99, hi_n99 = rhat_u - z99 * 0.205, rhat_u + z99 * 0.205
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Bootstrap distribution of the correlation between uniform malevolence and penalty yards for 28 NFL teams with the percentile and normal-based 99 percent intervals marked
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
sns.histplot(x=bmu, bins=45, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
ax.axvline(rhat_u, color="black", lw=1.5)
for v in (lo_p99, hi_p99):
    ax.axvline(v, color="#c44e52", ls="--", lw=1.2)
for v in (lo_n99, hi_n99):
    ax.axvline(v, color="#55a868", ls=":", lw=1.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Bootstrap sample correlations")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
pd.Series({"Observed r": round(rhat_u, 3),
           "Bootstrap mean / median": f"({bmu.mean():.3f}, {np.median(bmu):.3f})",
           "Bootstrap SE (5000 samples)": round(se_u, 3),
           "SE shown in Figure 5.23": 0.205,
           "(a) 99% normal interval": f"({lo_n99:.3f}, {hi_n99:.3f})",
           "99% percentile interval (comparison)": f"({lo_p99:.3f}, {hi_p99:.3f})"}).to_string()
```

- **(a)** Using the original $r = 0.43$ and the SE = 0.205 from Figure 5.23
  with $z^* = 2.576$ for 99% confidence:
  $0.43 \pm 2.576(0.205) = 0.43 \pm 0.528$ gives **(−0.098, 0.958)**. (Our
  own 5000-sample bootstrap reproduces the figure: mean 0.397, SE ≈ 0.207,
  percentile interval (−0.221, 0.792) vs the book's (−0.224, 0.788).)
- **(b)** The normal-based interval (−0.098, 0.958) is symmetric about
  $r = 0.43$, while the percentile interval (−0.224, 0.788) is not — it is
  shifted noticeably left. **The reason is skew: the bootstrap distribution
  has a long left tail** (its mean, 0.397, sits below the median ≈ 0.42, and
  the dots trail down past −0.4). A normal model, which is symmetric,
  cannot capture that left tail, so the symmetric $z^*$ interval misses it:
  it cuts off the low end too early and stretches the high end too far. When
  the bootstrap distribution is skewed, the percentile interval is the more
  trustworthy of the two.

:::
